sections.description: This section introduces the patient's clinical presentation, covering the background of Behçet's disease needed to contextualize the case, the presenting symptoms and physical examination findings, and the initial laboratory abnormalities that prompted further investigation. It establishes the clinical picture that led clinicians to suspect a multisystem inflammatory process and outlines the significance of the concurrent mucocutaneous and neurological findings at presentation.
subtopics: Overview of Behçet's disease: epidemiology, multisystem nature, and typical clinical course
Neurological involvement in BD: timing, prevalence, and spectrum of neuro-BD presentations
Case presentation: fever, headache, mucocutaneous lesions, and systemic symptoms in a man in his 60s
Physical examination findings: oral aphthae, folliculitis-like rashes, genital ulcer, and euvolemic status
Initial laboratory abnormalities: severe hyponatremia, elevated inflammatory markers, elevated CK, and hyperglycemia
Clinical significance of concurrent mucocutaneous lesions and neurological symptoms at initial presentation

sections.description: This section details the systematic diagnostic process, from the initial broad differential diagnosis for fever, headache, and hyponatremia, through the stepwise exclusion of infectious, neoplastic, and autoimmune etiologies, to the establishment of definite BD and acute neuro-BD. It covers the interpretation of CSF analysis, neuroimaging, and the application of the International Criteria for Behçet's Disease, emphasizing how clinicians navigated diagnostic uncertainty when genital ulcers were initially absent.
subtopics: Broad initial differential diagnosis for fever, headache, and hyponatremia
Exclusion of infectious causes: viral meningoencephalitis (HSV, VZV), bacterial meningitis, and tuberculous meningitis
Exclusion of neoplastic causes: primary CNS malignancy and haematological malignancy
Exclusion of autoimmune and granulomatous diseases: connective tissue disorders and neurosarcoidosis
CSF analysis in neuro-BD: aseptic meningitis pattern, lymphocytic pleocytosis, and negative microbiological workup
Role and limitations of brain MRI in acute neuro-BD: normal imaging does not exclude the diagnosis
Application of the International Criteria for Behçet's Disease: scoring system and diagnostic threshold
Diagnostic significance of HLA-B51 and its limited role in confirming BD
Challenges of early diagnosis when genital ulcers are absent and the importance of clinical pattern recognition

sections.section_title: SIADH: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Association with Neuro-BD
sections.description: This section focuses on the endocrine complication of SIADH, covering its diagnostic criteria, the laboratory evaluation that confirmed the diagnosis, and the proposed pathophysiological link between CNS inflammation in neuro-BD and dysregulated ADH secretion. It also addresses the underrecognized clinical consequences of severe hyponatremia observed in this case, including persistent hiccups and rhabdomyolysis.
subtopics: Diagnostic criteria for SIADH: hypo-osmolar hyponatremia, euvolemia, elevated urinary sodium and osmolality, and elevated ADH
Exclusion of other causes of hyponatremia: adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, and renal dysfunction
Endocrine evaluation: normal cortisol, TSH, and free T4 as exclusionary tests
Pathophysiology of SIADH in CNS inflammation: the role of IL-6 in stimulating ADH release
Proposed mechanism linking neuro-BD-associated CNS inflammation to SIADH via IL-6-mediated pathways
Evidence for elevated IL-6 in neuro-BD and its relevance to ADH dysregulation
Clinical complications of severe hyponatremia: persistent hiccups as a clue to CNS inflammation and SIADH
Rhabdomyolysis as an underrecognized complication of profound hyponatremia

sections.description: This section covers the therapeutic approach, beginning with empirical antimicrobial coverage during diagnostic uncertainty, transitioning to targeted colchicine monotherapy after the diagnosis of BD and neuro-BD was established, and the conservative management of SIADH with fluid restriction. It explains the rationale for avoiding systemic corticosteroids and the pharmacological mechanism by which colchicine may address both mucocutaneous and neurological manifestations.
subtopics: Empirical antimicrobial therapy: rationale for cefepime and acyclovir during diagnostic uncertainty
Discontinuation of empirical treatments after exclusion of infectious causes
Colchicine pharmacology: mechanism of anti-inflammatory action via neutrophil inhibition and cytokine suppression (IL-1β, IL-6)
Colchicine in BD: established role for mucocutaneous manifestations and conventional limitations for neuro-BD
Rationale for colchicine monotherapy in this case: avoidance of corticosteroids and immunosuppressants
Evidence and controversy regarding colchicine for acute neuro-BD: systematic review findings and case reports
Topical management of mucocutaneous lesions: corticosteroid ointment and silver sulfadiazine cream
Conservative management of SIADH: fluid restriction, daily sodium monitoring, and avoidance of rapid correction
Why hypertonic saline and vasopressin receptor antagonists were not required

sections.section_title: Clinical Outcome, Follow-up, and Key Lessons
sections.description: This section covers the patient's clinical course following treatment initiation, including the timeline of symptom resolution and normalization of laboratory abnormalities, the long-term follow-up demonstrating sustained remission, and the broader clinical lessons derived from this case. It emphasizes the importance of recognizing the concurrent diagnosis of BD and neuro-BD, the potential association between neuro-BD and SIADH, and the need for judicious diagnostic testing.
subtopics: Timeline of clinical improvement following colchicine initiation: fever, appetite, neurological symptoms, and mucocutaneous lesions
Normalization of serum sodium and ADH levels by day 16
Resolution of elevated CK and inflammatory markers
Hospital course: one-month admission, rehabilitation, and discharge planning
Long-term follow-up: four years of colchicine therapy without recurrence of BD or neurological symptoms
Subsequent management of type 2 diabetes after BD stabilization
Clinical lesson: recognizing concurrent BD and neuro-BD as a rare but important presentation
Clinical lesson: considering SIADH in patients with neuro-BD presenting with hyponatremia
Clinical lesson: the value of pattern recognition over indiscriminate diagnostic testing
Clinical lesson: colchicine as a potential alternative to corticosteroids in selected cases of acute neuro-BD
Limitations: inability to establish a definitive causal link between neuro-BD and SIADH
